Lanza's salamander, Salamandra lanzai, is a viviparous urodele inhabiting high-altitude environments in the southwestern Alps, where low temperatures profoundly shape its life history. At the cold temperatures prevailing in its subterranean gestation sites, around 3 °C [T = 3 °C], embryonic development is exceptionally protracted. Field observations suggest that the offspring, fully formed at birth, possess a snout-vent length of approximately 1.3 cm [Lb = approximately 1.3 cm] and a corresponding wet body mass of about 0.125 grams [Wwb = about 0.125 grams]. This extended intrauterine period, lasting about 3.5 years [ab = about 3.5 years] at the same thermal regime, reflects the extreme metabolic constraints imposed by persisten at a temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C]t cold. The resulting age at birth, one of the longest recorded among European salamandrids, appears to be an adaptation to a harsh, resource-limited alpine environment. Neonates are thus born as miniature versions of the adults, bypassing an aquatic larval stage entirely, an evolutionary strategy that reduces offspring mortality but demands a substantial energetic investment by the female over several consecutive years.

Following parturition, the newborn salamanders begin a gradual, independent growth phase in the cold, humid microhabitats of alpine screes and meadows. The time elapsed from birth until the completion of metamorphosis, which in this species is a subtle developmental transition rather than a dramatic aquatic-to-terrestrial shift, has been estimated at approximately 4.5 months from birth  when measured at a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. At this point, the juvenile salamanders have achieved a snout-vent length of 3.4 cm  and a wet weight of 1.5 grams . These measurements indicate a relatively slow juvenile growth rate compared to lower-elevation congeners, likely a consequence of limited thermal opportunities for foraging and digestion. The post-metamorphic juveniles then enter a protracted period of somatic growth before reaching the size thresholds required for reproductive maturation, a phase during which they must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to survive multiple alpine winters.

Males of Salamandra lanzai achieve sexual maturity at a smaller body size and at a younger age than their female counterparts, a pattern typical of many polygynous amphibians. The age at which males first become capable of reproduction, or puberty, is estimated to be 4 years since birth [tp = 4 years since birth] at an average ambient temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C]. At this point, the snout-vent length of pubertal males is recorded at 6.6 cm [Lp = 6.6 cm], and their body mass reaches a wet weight of 8.5 grams [Wwp = 8.5 grams]. In contrast, females are reported to reach puberty somewhat later, at 6 years since birth [tp = 6 years since birth] under the same thermal conditions of 3 °C [T = 3 °C], suggesting a divergent life-history strategy that prioritizes extended somatic growth to maximize future fecundity. At the onset of female reproductive maturation, the snout-vent length is roughly 7.0 cm [Lp = roughly 7.0 cm] and the wet body mass is 8 grams [Wwp = 8 grams], indicating that females begin breeding at a similar mass to males despite their later age.

As individuals continue to grow after attaining sexual maturity, they slowly approach their ultimate body size. The maximum snout-vent length recorded for adult females is 9.1 cm [Li = 9.1 cm], while adult males achieve a slightly greater maximum snout-vent length of 9.3 cm [Li = 9.3 cm]. This modest sexual dimorphism in body length is mirrored in the ultimate wet weight, where females reach a maximum of 20 grams [Wwi = 20 grams] and males attain a peak of 15.5 grams [Wwi = 15.5 grams]. The larger ultimate mass of females is almost certainly related to the demands of gestation, as females must support developing young for multiple years. The reproductive output of a fully grown female, weighing around 25.3 grams, is constrained by the lengthy gestation period; she produces a small clutch of up to 6 young [N_R_i = clutch of up to 6 young] approximately every 3.5 years [F_R_i = approximately every 3.5 years] at 3 °C [T = 3 °C], resulting in one of the lowest documented reproductive rates among terrestrial amphibians. This translates to an annual reproduction rate of about 1.7 young per year [Ri = about 1.7 young per year].

The exceptionally slow pace of life in Salamandra lanzai culminates in an impressive longevity. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, which is presumably achieved only by individuals that successfully avoid predation and disease for many decades in the alpine environment, is 24 years [am = 24 years] at a mean temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C]. This extreme lifespan, coupled with the long age at first reproduction, reflects a life-history strategy strongly skewed toward iteroparity and high adult survival. When compared to its lower-elevation congener Salamandra salamandra, which typically lives for about a decade, the Lanza's salamander appears to have traded rapid development and high annual fecundity for extreme longevity and a very low but consistent annual reproductive rate. These demographic traits provide a striking example of how persistent cold temperatures can fundamentally slow the physiological clock and reshape the evolution of life-history schedules in ectothermic vertebrates.
